Forward-looking guidance belongs to fictional executives (own_claim=false); the author's own opening paragraph is present-tense.

Logged: the Prenuvo screening claim, the polls-are-wrong call and its restatements, a toss-up call, and a hedged anticipation of false post-election claims.
Julius Caesar funeral-oration parody about Sean Combs, Eric Adams, Elon Musk and Bluesky; past and present satire, no forward-looking claim.

Review of a two-site open-label SAINT feasibility trial in treatment-refractory bipolar I depression (Li et al. 2024) after the Raj et al. pilot. One present-tense efficacy assessment logged with forward_looking=false; 'I look forward to more data' and 'Let's get it to reach everybody' are wishes, not logged.

statements.quote: Just pay more for mental health care ... it will be hard to argue you are paying less.
statements.context: Closing of a post on mental health parity enforcement (Linda Gomez of the Employee Benefits Security Administration, interviewed by Clear Health Costs, says plans must treat mental health and medical claims the same). The author proposes, tongue in cheek, that payers simply pay more for mental health care; then payers could not be accused of paying less and would satisfy parity. He adds 'I didn't say it would be a good solution.'
statements.note: Tongue-in-cheek proposal ('be forewarned, is dumb'); the conditional mechanism (paying more satisfies parity) reads as a real belief. Quote joins the proposal and its consequence.

statements.quote: More transparency would put this kind of speculation to rest, but that's not what we've gotten from that sizeable corporate entity, and I doubt we will.
statements.context: Closing of a post that uses TikTok viewer geography (over 223,000 views from the Philippines on a video about UnitedHealthcare layoffs) to infer the scale of UnitedHealthcare/Optum's offshore workforce, after noting that UnitedHealthcare does not report US layoffs under the federal WARN Act. The author expects no more transparency from the company.
statements.note: Negative call: the author does not expect UnitedHealthcare to become transparent about layoffs or offshore staffing.

statements.quote: More tips in this thrilling series tomorrow!
statements.context: Part three of the author's mentalization-based treatment (MBT) visual guide, on 'too hot' emotional states (psychic equivalence and teleological mode, renamed 'feelings equal facts' and 'prove-it mode'). Sign-off promising the next installment the following day.
statements.note: Newsletter programming promise about the author's own publication (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: In what may be the last chance to use a video of Beyonce and Destiny's Child without wincing
statements.context: Same MBT post; the author introduces the Destiny's Child song 'Say My Name' as an example of hot emotions and quips that this may be the last chance to use a Beyonce video 'without wincing'. The reason is not stated.
statements.note: Throwaway quip implying Beyonce references will soon become awkward; not a real forecast. Logged for completeness.

statements.quote: Practically, if we don't take care of people who are violent or at risk of becoming violent, they're going to be violent. And they're going to participate in trauma and exploitation. We will all suffer in the aftermath.
statements.context: Essay prompted by the sex-trafficking indictment of former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO Michael Jeffries and the Sean Combs allegations; the author argues trauma propagates ('hurt people hurt people'). Conditional societal claim: without care for violent or at-risk people, violence, trauma and exploitation follow and everyone suffers.
statements.note: Conditional generalization about violence prevention; no specific event, actor or date.

statements.quote: Appropriate resources for law enforcement and courts means the distance between predation and getting what's coming to you might shrink enough for potential evil-doers to think twice. Or, better yet, victims will be allowed resolution sooner.
statements.context: Same essay; the author argues court delays re-traumatize victims (he cites his own harassment lawsuit filed April 11, 2023, still awaiting a first ruling). Conditional: with more court and law-enforcement resources, deterrence and faster resolution for victims might follow.
statements.note: Conditional on funding for courts and law enforcement; policy advocacy with a hedged predictive reading.

statements.quote: They are doomed to wait years even after they get the courage to file something
statements.context: Same essay. Generalization that people who rely on legal processes to resolve complaints against predators will wait years for resolution, contrasted with predators who 'don't follow the law' and take swift revenge (Sean Combs accused of firebombing Kid Cudi).
statements.note: Borderline: standing generalization about court delays rather than a dated call; logged for recall.

statements.quote: Our editorial point of view is that medical devices that modulate the brain will be the future.
statements.context: Review of the Nature Medicine phase 2 fully remote sham-controlled trial of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (Flow Neuroscience device; the author nicknames it HEAD-TRIP, real name EMPOWER). Opening editorial stance: brain-modulating medical devices, not oral medicines, will be the future of treatment.
statements.note: Restates a recurring editorial thesis of the newsletter; contrasted with Elon Musk's 'it's coming' self-driving promises.

statements.quote: Despite being an at-home trial, it probably doesn't generalize to Medicaid populations easily, for example.
statements.context: Same tDCS review; after listing the trial's exclusion criteria (no prior ketamine or esketamine, no psychiatric hospitalization, no bipolar, PTSD, OCD or primary anxiety diagnoses, a current psychiatrist and an up-to-date phone required), the author judges the results unlikely to generalize to Medicaid populations.
statements.note: Borderline: generalizability judgment about the EMPOWER trial; implicitly a call about results in broader, sicker populations.

statements.quote: It also calls for subsequent trials to answer these questions for practicing clinicians if the device is approved.
statements.context: Same tDCS review; the author says the narrow inclusion criteria mean further trials will be needed to guide clinicians if the Flow device is approved, and advocates broader criteria for the phase 3 trial.
statements.note: Advice; the conditional 'if the device is approved' treats approval as possible but is not a prediction. Logged for completeness.

statements.quote: The sham? It will need to be improved to preserve the blind in future trials!
statements.context: Same review; functional unblinding (77.6% of the active arm and 59.3% of the sham arm guessed active) and skin redness in the active arm revealed group assignment. The author says the sham condition will need improvement in future tDCS trials.
statements.note: Mostly normative (a design requirement) with a weak predictive reading about future tDCS trials.

statements.quote: And we shouldn't expect that from tDCS, based on prior studies.
statements.context: Same review; the author asks whether home tDCS is 'at home SAINT TMS' and answers no: tDCS should not be expected to match SAINT-level efficacy, based on prior studies (pooled tDCS effect size 0.46; this trial 0.37).
statements.note: Negative expectation: tDCS will not reach SAINT-like effect sizes.

statements.context: Satirical post written as a corporate product-shutdown notice signed 'The Hopes and Dreams Team', in which 'hope' is the discontinued program, 'the tortured' are users and 'tormentors' are creators; the dates apparently mirror a real platform wind-down notice. Opening line: the fictional program winds down in February 2025.
entities: Hope for A Better Life (fictional program)
statements.note: Parody; fictional speaker. The date is in-fiction and not the author's forecast.

statements.quote: Also, for your calendar planning purposes, please note that our first quarter fiscal year 2025 earnings conference call has been tentatively scheduled for Tuesday, January 28th, 2025.
statements.context: Halloween satire: the Q4 and full-year 2024 earnings call of 'Last Choice Blood Care Partners' (LastChoice BloodCare), a publicly traded vampire-coven roll-up, apparently parodying a real Q4 fiscal 2024 earnings call (returning CEO, 'Back to Blood' turnaround plan, Rewards membership of 33.8 million, 14% China decline, 'four minutes or less' service goal). The fictional head of investor relations, Brett Whiteman, gives the date of the next earnings call.
statements.note: Fiction; date belongs to a parody company and may mirror the parodied company's real schedule. Not the author's forecast.

statements.quote: I have confidence in our ability to turn around our bloodline’s precipitous decline.
statements.context: Halloween satire: the Q4 and full-year 2024 earnings call of 'Last Choice Blood Care Partners' (LastChoice BloodCare), a publicly traded vampire-coven roll-up, apparently parodying a real Q4 fiscal 2024 earnings call (returning CEO, 'Back to Blood' turnaround plan, Rewards membership of 33.8 million, 14% China decline, 'four minutes or less' service goal). The fictional CFO, Maria Soprano, closes her results section (volume down 3%, China down 14%) with turnaround confidence.
statements.note: Fiction; turnaround guidance voiced by a parody executive. The allegorical target (private-equity roll-ups) is not itself forecast here.

statements.quote: My experience tells me that when we get Back to our core identity and consistently demand a great experience for ourselves first, and if we are demanding enough, the humans will return to our lairs. Our problems are fixable.
statements.context: Halloween satire: the Q4 and full-year 2024 earnings call of 'Last Choice Blood Care Partners' (LastChoice BloodCare), a publicly traded vampire-coven roll-up, apparently parodying a real Q4 fiscal 2024 earnings call (returning CEO, 'Back to Blood' turnaround plan, Rewards membership of 33.8 million, 14% China decline, 'four minutes or less' service goal). 'Dracula', chairman and chief vampire officer, lays out the 'Back to Blood' plan and predicts customers ('the humans') will return.
statements.note: Fiction; conditional turnaround claim by a parody executive. Other in-fiction plans ('sharing more ... shortly', 'four minutes or less', 'some things will take some time') not logged separately.

statements.quote: I think that will take technology and better contracts
statements.context: Roundup of the author's own research and clinical projects (Fermata, Acacia Clinics, Psyrin, Videra Health). Opening: the author calls himself 'an enthusiast for the future to be better' and thinks that better future will require technology and better (payer) contracts.
statements.note: Vague structural claim about what improvement in mental health care will require.

statements.quote: We will soon enroll subjects in a vocal biomarker trial to evaluate responses to rapid-acting mental health treatments ... This trial will enroll in Brooklyn and Sunnyvale.
statements.context: Same roundup, bullet list of ongoing research at the author's organizations. Announces an upcoming vocal biomarker trial sponsored by Psyrin, to enroll in Brooklyn (Fermata) and Sunnyvale (Acacia Clinics). Quote skips the parenthetical '(study sponsor: Psyrin )'.
statements.note: Own-organization trial plan (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: If you live near Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, our partners at Living Water Clinics are also bringing neuromodulation to your community
statements.context: Same roundup, under 'other colossal developments' (Fermata in-network with TRICARE and Cigna). A partner non-profit, Living Water Clinics, is bringing neuromodulation treatment to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.
statements.note: Borderline: present-progressive rollout announcement about a partner; logged for recall.

statements.quote: This is why expensive and error-prone universal screening like preneuvo is a terrible idea. The test will get it wrong enough that people will be subjected to subsequent risk from excessive and invasive workups to follow up on an incidental finding that wouldn't have mattered.
statements.context: Statistics essay on sampling, sensitivity and specificity, applied to election polls. Aside on universal screening: whole-body screening like Prenuvo ('preneuvo') will produce enough false positives that people will face risk from invasive follow-up workups.
statements.note: General predictive claim about the consequences of universal screening; a recurring position of the author.

statements.quote: This phenomenon means that the polls for this election are almost certainly wrong
statements.context: Same essay, published the day before the 2024 US presidential election. Following Nate Silver's 'herding' argument (swing-state polls cluster too tightly around 50-50 to be honest samples with a 3-4% margin of error), the author concludes the polls are almost certainly wrong, that is, carry a systematic error.
statements.note: Endorsed restatement of Nate Silver's herding argument; resolves against the November 5, 2024 results versus final polls. Trump and Harris are named only in the quoted Silver passage.

statements.quote: Nate points out that the overabundance of polls showing this to be a very close race is evidence that the polls are wrong—they aren’t normally distributed! This means there is a systematic bias in the results we are seeing.
statements.context: Same essay, right after a quoted Silver Bulletin passage ('a systematic polling error is always possible, perhaps especially if you think pollsters are herding'; author adds 'Emphasis mine'). The author restates and adopts the claim: the polls carry a systematic bias.
statements.note: Restatement of the previous call, anchored to the quoted third-party (Nate Silver) forecast that the author adopts.

statements.quote: The election could go either way.
statements.context: Same essay; after arguing the polls are herded and wrong, the author declines to call the 2024 US presidential race and urges readers to vote.
statements.note: Explicit toss-up call; the author says he supports 'Candidate A' but does not predict the winner.

statements.quote: Your vote counts—especially when the polls are highly likely to be inaccurate, as is currently the case.
statements.context: Same essay, final line after 'GO OUT AND VOTE'. Restates that the pre-election polls are highly likely to be inaccurate.
statements.note: Restatement of the poll-error call earlier in the same post.

statements.quote: That is one way to reduce the risk of claims of voter suppression or other nonsense that could allow a candidate to falsely claim things should have been otherwise.
statements.context: Same essay's closing plea to vote: a large, counted turnout reduces the risk that a candidate falsely claims voter suppression or that the result should have been otherwise.
statements.note: Hedged anticipation of false post-election claims by a candidate; borderline.

statements.quote: Today, we present yet more evidence that accelerated neuromodulation with fMRI guidance appears to be an effective treatment for bipolar depression.
statements.context: Review of a two-site open-label feasibility trial of SAINT (Stanford Accelerated Intelligent Neuromodulation Therapy) in treatment-refractory bipolar I depression (60% response; Li et al. 2024, Journal of Affective Disorders), following the Raj et al. seven-patient pilot. Opening claim that fMRI-guided accelerated TMS appears effective in bipolar depression, where antidepressants and conventional TMS have not worked.
statements.note: Present-tense evidence assessment, not a dated call; logged because the efficacy claim is testable by future replication (author: 'Until a study is replicated, it's just a magic trick').
